passage: Abebe stood in the operations manager's doorway holding a folder. Three deliveries to the same customer had gone out wrong, and the manager had just said it was Abebe's team, so Abebe's fault. Yara, the junior dispatcher, had made the errors and sat at her desk down the hall, pretending to read. "I own that I didn't catch the pattern sooner," Abebe said. "But I sat with Yara twice and went through the checklist, and here are the dates. She has been carrying sixty orders a day alone since March. I'd like a second person on the evening shift." The manager frowned at the folder, then said they would look at the rosters on Monday. Abebe never once blamed Yara aloud, and walked back down the hall with a tight jaw.

qa.q: How many times had Abebe sat with Yara to go through the checklist?
What does Abebe's tight jaw suggest as Abebe walks back down the hall?
qa.a: Abebe is tense and probably still stung by the blame, even after making a calm case.

qa.q: What did Abebe ask the manager for, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: A second person on the evening shift, because Yara had been carrying sixty orders a day alone.

qa.q: How might Yara have felt sitting at her desk pretending to read?
qa.a: Yara may have been anxious and ashamed, aware the errors were hers and unsure whether she would be blamed.

grounding: A boss blames a lead for a junior's failures, and the lead owns their part, shows the coaching given and asks for resourcing without blaming the junior.

passage:
HR business partner's note, meeting between Mr. Kapoor (regional head) and Yogesh (team lead), Thursday.

Mr. Kapoor opened by saying the team's Q2 targets were missed "because of your junior, Rekha, and your poor supervision". He raised his voice twice.

Yogesh's face was tight, but his voice stayed even. He said, "The shortfall is on my team, so I own it." He then described the coaching he had given Rekha: weekly reviews since April, a written checklist, and two joint client calls. He produced the review notes.

He did not blame Rekha. When Mr. Kapoor said, "So she's the weak link," Yogesh replied, "She's improving. Our real gap is that I'm covering two territories with three people."

He asked for one more field executive, or a reduced target for Q3.

Mr. Kapoor paused, then asked for a written staffing proposal by Monday. I will follow up on the proposal and on Rekha's development plan.

qa.q: How many people was Yogesh covering two territories with?
qa.a: He was covering two territories with three people.

qa.q: What did Yogesh's tight face but even voice suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggested he felt stung and defensive at being blamed, but chose to stay calm.

qa.q: How did Yogesh handle the blame responsibly?
qa.a: He owned the shortfall, showed the coaching he had given, refused to scapegoat Rekha, and asked for resourcing support.

qa.q: How might Rekha have been affected if Yogesh had blamed her?
qa.a: Rekha could have been unfairly labelled as the weak link, harming her confidence and career while she was still improving.

grounding: An HR note shows a team lead blamed by his boss for a junior's failures, who takes responsibility, explains his coaching, asks for resourcing and does not scapegoat the junior.

passage:
Wednesday.

Today Mr. Iyer called me into his cabin and said, "Gautam missed the Delhi deadline, and that's on you, Abhinav. What kind of lead lets this happen?"

My heart was pounding. Everything in me wanted to say, "Gautam didn't tell me until the last day! It's his fault!" It would have been partly true. And it would have thrown a twenty-three-year-old under the bus to save my own skin.

What I said instead: "You're right that I'm responsible for the team's deadlines. I checked in with Gautam every Monday and he said it was on track. I should have asked to see the actual work, not just status updates. I'll do that from now on."

Then: "Honestly, sir, one junior on three client projects is too much. Can we get an intern or push one project back?"

Mr. Iyer grunted. "Send me a proposal."

I walked out shaky, but I'm Abhinav, and I didn't sell Gautam out. That matters to me.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when Mr. Iyer blamed him?
qa.a: Abhinav's heart was pounding with anger and fear, and the temptation was to put all the blame on Gautam.

qa.q: Why was Abhinav's answer wiser than blaming Gautam?
qa.a: Abhinav owned that part, explained the coaching given and what to change, and asked for resources, instead of scapegoating a junior.

qa.q: How might Gautam have been affected if Abhinav had blamed him?
qa.a: Gautam, a young junior, could have been unfairly singled out and lost confidence, while the real resourcing problem stayed hidden.

grounding: A diary entry shows a team lead blamed by the boss for a junior's missed deadline, who takes responsibility for their own part, explains the coaching given, asks for resources and does not scapegoat the junior.
